_comment: Term-level pages, one per scenario category. The category page targets the situation ('how to order a beer in Spain'); these target the word ('what does caña mean'), which is a different search and a shorter one. Each term must carry its own weight — a gloss, why it matters, and the real line from the deck it appears in — because a page of bare definitions is a doorway page and gets treated as one.

beer-food.title: Spanish bar words
beer-food.heading: Spanish bar words you'll actually hear
beer-food.blurb: The words that come at you across a Spanish bar, what each one means, and the line it turns up in.

terms.note: The default order in Spain. Asking for 'una cerveza' works but marks you out; asking for 'una caña' doesn't.
Casual and extremely common. Fine with bar staff and strangers your own age; use the full 'por favor' with older people.
The most-used word in Spain. It confirms, it agrees, it ends a conversation. You'll hear it doubled — 'vale, vale' — when someone wants you to stop talking.
In much of Spain it arrives free with a drink; in Madrid and the south that's more likely than in Barcelona. You can also order one outright.
terms.heardIn: Sí: una tapa de tortilla, porfa.

terms.note: The opposite is 'de botella', bottled. This is the first thing they'll ask after you order a beer.
How beer gets described rather than by brand. 'Rubia' is the standard pale lager you'd expect.

terms.gloss: An espresso cut with a splash of warm milk.
terms.note: Between a 'solo' (straight espresso) and a 'café con leche' (half milk). Ordering a latte by name will get you a confused look.
Nobody brings it unprompted — in Spain that would be rushing you out. You ask.
The opposite of 'para aquí', for here. Asked at counters and cafés constantly.
Bar staff shorthand once your order is in. You don't say it — you just need to recognise it.

terms.gloss: Boss — a friendly way to address staff.
terms.note: Warm rather than rude, but it's familiar. Safe in a neighbourhood bar, less so in a smart restaurant.

getting-around.title: Spanish taxi & metro words
getting-around.heading: Spanish taxi and metro words you'll actually hear
getting-around.blurb: The words on the signs and in the driver's mouth, what each one means, and the line it turns up in.

terms.note: 'Parada' is any stop — a taxi rank, a bus stop, a metro stop. Context does the rest.
terms.heardIn: Perdona, ¿dónde está la parada de taxis?

terms.note: Spanish taxis are metered and legally have to run it. Asking for it switched on is normal and not an accusation.
Worth asking for if you've left something behind — the ride is traceable from it.
The single most useful metro word in Spain. It's a verb phrase, not a noun you'd see alone on a sign.

terms.gloss: Transfer — the word on the signs.
terms.note: This is what you follow overhead once you're inside the station. You ask for 'transbordo' and you follow 'Correspondencia'.
Going the wrong way is fixed by changing andén, not by leaving the station.
terms.heardIn: Te bajas en la siguiente y cambias de andén.

terms.gloss: Toward — how Spanish metro lines are labelled.
terms.note: Lines aren't 'northbound'; they're named after the last station. You need the direction, not just the line number.
From 'bajarse'. You'll hear it as instruction rather than suggestion, which is normal and not rude.
Distance on the metro gets measured in stops, not minutes.
The default half of every set of directions you'll be given on the street.
terms.heardIn: Sí, todo recto y a la izquierda.

terms.gloss: At the far end / down the back.
terms.note: Used for the end of a street, a corridor, or a bar. It means further than you think.

restaurant.title: Spanish restaurant words
restaurant.heading: Spanish restaurant words you'll actually hear
restaurant.blurb: What the waiter is asking you, what's on the plate, and how the bill gets split.

terms.note: The first thing said to you at the door, often as a single word with a raised eyebrow.

terms.gloss: How many of you are there?
terms.note: Answered with 'somos' — 'somos dos'. Not 'vamos'.
Spanish meals get ordered in waves rather than as courses, so this opens the order rather than naming a starter.
The default assumption in Spain. The waiter asking this isn't being nosy — it changes how the food is plated.

terms.gloss: The most typical thing — the local speciality.
terms.note: The single best question in the deck. It gets you what the place is actually good at.
terms.heardIn: ¿Qué es lo más típico de aquí?

terms.note: One of the three things named when you ask what's typical, alongside tortilla and pulpo.
terms.heardIn: La tortilla / las croquetas / el pulpo…

terms.note: The whole allergy and preference conversation hangs off this one word: 'sin gluten', 'sin cebolla', 'sin lactosa'.
What you'll hear when there's no table. Not a negotiation.

terms.gloss: To charge — the verb for taking payment.
terms.note: Spanish uses 'cobrar' where English says 'take payment'. '¿Me cobras?' is how you flag for the bill.
Normal and unremarkable in Spain, though a big table may be asked to settle up together.

terms.gloss: I've made a mistake / got mixed up.
terms.note: What the waiter says when the plate was for another table. Recognising it saves the awkward pause.
terms.heardIn: Uy, perdona, me he confundido de mesa.
